passage: Thursday, 9:40 pm. Anand, you did it again. Rohit stopped by my desk at four and I spent forty minutes drawing little boxes on a notepad for him, laughing about the time I broke a whole workbook in my first year. Disha waited beside the printer with her question, and I said "later, okay?" Later never came. She left at six, clutching her laptop bag. Tonight I counted: Rohit got three long sessions this week, Disha got one two-minute reply. Her work is not worse, it is just slower to explain itself, and talking with her costs me more effort. Tomorrow: fifteen minutes each on the calendar, the same ask of both, a short written status. I will judge the drafts, not how easy the chat felt. A bit embarrassed writing this down.

qa.q: How many long sessions did Rohit get this week, according to Anand's count?
qa.a: Rohit got three long sessions this week.

qa.q: Why does Anand feel embarrassed while writing the entry?
qa.a: Anand has caught a bias: time went to the junior who felt comfortable, while Disha got one two-minute reply.

qa.q: What step does Anand plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: Put fifteen minutes each for Rohit and Disha on the calendar and ask both for the same short written status.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt leaving at six with her bag held to her chest?
qa.a: Disha may have felt overlooked and unsure whether her questions were welcome.

grounding: The narrator notices favouring the junior who feels like them, and plans equal time and the same expectations for both juniors.

passage:
At the nursing station of the cardiac ward, Minakshi had two new juniors. Vandana was quick, chatty and asked the questions Minakshi herself had asked ten years ago. Kuldeep was quiet, a little stiff, and never laughed at her jokes.

One evening, filling the duty chart, Minakshi noticed something. She had spent four hours that week teaching Vandana the new monitors. Kuldeep had had twenty minutes. And in her head she had already written him off as "slow".

She felt uncomfortable. When had she last actually looked at his work?

She pulled out the week's charts. Kuldeep's notes were the most complete on the ward. He had caught a medication clash that the doctor had missed.

The next morning, Minakshi changed the chart: one hour of teaching each for both juniors, every Tuesday. She told Kuldeep, "Your notes caught that clash. That was excellent work." He looked surprised, and then, for the first time, he smiled.

qa.q: How many hours had Minakshi spent teaching Vandana the new monitors that week?
What did Minakshi feel when she saw how unevenly she had divided her time?
qa.a: Minakshi felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, realising she had written Kuldeep off.

qa.q: How did Minakshi correct her bias?
qa.a: She checked the evidence of Kuldeep's work, gave both juniors equal teaching time, and praised his work specifically.

qa.q: How might Kuldeep have felt before Minakshi noticed his work?
qa.a: Kuldeep probably felt overlooked and invisible, which may be why he seemed stiff.

grounding: The passage shows a senior nurse who notices she favours the junior who reminds her of herself, catches the bias, gives equal time and judges by evidence.

passage:
Dear Rekha ma'am,

You once told me the hardest part of managing is noticing your own blind spots. I've found one, and I'm writing to you because you'll understand.

I have two juniors. Priyal is loud, fast and funny, a lot like I was at twenty-two. Ayesha is careful and quiet, and she asks the same question twice. I realised this week that I've had lunch with Priyal four times this month and given Ayesha only emails. When the new client came, I gave it to Priyal without thinking.

Then I looked at their actual numbers. Ayesha's reports have zero errors. Priyal's have seven.

I felt ashamed. I've been judging by comfort, not by work.

So I've started a fixed thirty-minute meeting with each of them every Monday, with the same written goals. The next client goes to whoever is better suited, by evidence.

Thank you for teaching me to look.

Neelam

qa.q: How many errors were in Ayesha's reports?
How did Neelam feel after comparing the actual numbers?
qa.a: Neelam felt ashamed, realising the judging had been based on comfort, not work.

qa.q: What steps did Neelam take to be fair?
qa.a: A fixed thirty-minute weekly meeting with each junior, the same written goals, and assigning clients by evidence.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt being managed only by email?
qa.a: Ayesha may have felt ignored and less valued than Priyal, despite doing careful, error-free work.

grounding: A letter shows a young manager who catches a bias toward the junior who feels most familiar, and who gives each equal time and clear expectations and judges by evidence.
